# In Praise of the Unbroken

Flip a light switch. The light comes on. You have done this ten thousand times without thinking about it, and that is exactly the point. Behind the small click stands an immense, humming apparatus: power plants burning and spinning and splitting, transformers stepping voltage up and down, wires sagging across miles of dark countryside, and somewhere, right now, a grid operator watching a screen and balancing supply against demand second by second so the whole trembling system holds. The light coming on is not a trivial event. It is a miracle performed so reliably that we have forgotten it ever was one.

Consider the tap. Turn it and out comes water you can drink, in most of the developed world, without a second thought. Somewhere upstream there are reservoirs and treatment plants, technicians measuring chlorine and turbidity, pumps pushing pressure through pipes laid a century ago by men whose names nobody remembers. When a water main breaks in February, someone goes out at three in the morning and stands waist-deep in freezing mud to fix it. It is often said that clean water has saved more lives than all of medicine combined, and whether or not that is strictly provable, it is close enough to the truth to be humbling.

There is a whole parallel civilization that works while we sleep. The bakers who start at three so the bread exists by seven. The crews restocking grocery shelves so the store looks effortlessly full at dawn. The garbage trucks grinding through dark streets, the snowplows out before the storm has even ended, the overnight nurses and the delivery drivers. Every morning the world appears freshly made, as if by magic, and we accept it the way children accept breakfast—as something that simply arrives. It does not simply arrive. It is made, nightly, by people we rarely see.

The digital world is maintained the same way. More than ninety-five percent of intercontinental internet traffic travels through cables lying on the ocean floor, and there are ships whose entire job is to find those cables when they break, haul them up, and splice them back together. Data centers hum in the dark while someone swaps out failed hard drives. Anonymous programmers patch code written before they were born. Remember Y2K? An enormous, unfashionable, planet-wide effort fixed the problem so thoroughly that afterward people concluded it had never been real. That is the fate of perfect maintenance: it looks like nothing happened at all.

This is the paradox at the heart of it: we only ever notice the machinery when it fails. The bridge that holds is boring. The bridge that falls is on the news for a week. A clean floor says nothing; a dirty one speaks volumes. Health, as the saying goes, is the silence of the organs—you do not hear from your knees until something is wrong with them. Entropy is the default setting of the universe; things drift toward disorder, rust, and ruin. The unbroken state of the world is not natural. It is achieved, daily, by effort.

And yet our culture saves its applause for the opposite thing. We celebrate founders and inventors, disruptors and visionaries. We hold groundbreaking ceremonies with golden shovels and ribbon-cuttings with oversized scissors. The new highway gets a press release; the patched pothole gets nothing. Nobody holds a ceremony for the fortieth consecutive year of a bridge's inspection schedule. Maintenance budgets are always the first to be cut, precisely because their value is invisible—right up until the moment it isn't. We build shiny new things and let the old ones quietly rot, then act surprised when the rot eventually announces itself.

The same quiet work is happening inside you. Right now, your cells are proofreading your DNA and correcting their own copying errors, dismantling damaged proteins, sealing tiny wounds you never knew you had. Your immune system is, at this moment, neutralizing threats that will never rise to the level of a symptom. You are not a finished object. You are an ongoing project of repair, a building whose scaffolding never comes down. To be alive at all is to be continuously maintained.

Everything worth keeping works this way. A friendship is not a possession but a practice—kept alive by small repeated gestures, the text sent for no reason, the showing up. A marriage is a thing repaired daily or it is a thing slowly lost. Languages survive because people keep speaking them; institutions survive because people keep showing up to meetings and doing the tedious, unglamorous work of continuity. Whatever is loved must be tended. Tending is most of what love actually is.

I have started trying to notice the maintainers. The custodian who knows a building better than any executive ever will. The road crew on the shoulder at dusk, the utility worker on the pole after the storm, the technician who climbs the broadcast tower to change the red warning light so airplanes pass safely in the dark, the librarian repairing a torn page with archival tape. There is a deep dignity in this work and almost no glory in it, and those two facts together say something uncomfortable about what we choose to reward. We have built statues to generals. The people who keep the water clean mostly get neither statues nor thanks.

So here is a modest proposal: one day a year—or even one hour—spent noticing the unbroken. The floor is clean because someone cleaned it. The light came on because an enormous apparatus, tended by thousands of hands, delivered power to your wall at the exact instant you asked for it. The bridge held. The water ran clear. None of it was guaranteed; all of it was done. Gratitude, it turns out, is mostly a form of attention—a willingness to see the click of the switch, and then the whole humming world behind it.
